label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**Wanted: two people who can push a trolley**

In my first week on the Thursday tea trolley I tipped an entire jug of milk over it. A patient called Pat laughed so much that somebody had to fetch her a tissue, and she told me afterwards it was the best afternoon she had had in a month. I mention this so that you know the standard required.

I have been doing the trolley in the day therapy unit since March 2022. Before that I spent 41 years as a bookkeeper, most of them for a builders' merchant in Dereham, and then eighteen months being retired, which I was not very good at. I had no regular reason to leave the house most weeks and I drifted. Thursdays put a stop to that. I get at least as much out of the arrangement as anybody gets out of me, and anyone who thinks hospice volunteers are saintly has not seen me with a milk jug.

I am writing because we are short. The rota is meant to have six of us and since the summer it has had four. One moved to Sheffield to be nearer the grandchildren and another has had a knee operation. Neither can be blamed, but it leaves gaps, and the four of us are covering them.

I know what most people assume about volunteering here, because I assumed it too. Either it must be harrowing, or you must need some sort of training that ordinary people do not have. On a Thursday afternoon it is neither.

The day unit has somewhere between 14 and 18 patients in on a Thursday. Many come for the art group or the hand massage, and some come simply for the company. Most of them go home afterwards. It is noisy and rather jolly. Mr Hollis, a retired signalman, takes two sugars and tells me about the 1953 floods every week, slightly differently each time. I have stopped correcting the dates. The bourbon biscuits always go first, so we now hide a packet for the late group, and I would ask you to keep that to yourselves.

It would be dishonest to pretend every week is like that. Some Thursdays are hard. Somebody you have got used to seeing is not there, and you feel it. When that happens the staff look after us as carefully as they look after everyone else, and nobody expects you to carry on as though nothing had happened. But those days are the exception, and I would not want them to put you off.

As for skill, you do not need any nursing knowledge whatsoever. You need to be able to push a trolley, remember who takes what, and listen. Four decades of keeping ledgers straight has turned out to be handy for remembering who takes what, but I am assured that other careers will do.

The commitment is one Thursday a fortnight, from 1.30 to 4pm. Before you start, Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, takes you through an induction which lasts about two hours. There is also a short food hygiene course to do online, which the hospice pays for. That is the whole of it.

If you think you might be interested, or are only curious, there is a volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room. There will be tea and biscuits and no obligation of any kind. If you cannot manage that date, ring Bridget on the volunteering line and she will tell you anything you want to know.

We need two people. I should very much like to see at least that many of you in the Willow Room on the 24th, and I will see what I can do about the bourbons.

---

Two things to check before this goes up:

- **Phone number:** you didn't give me the volunteering line number, so it needs adding where Bridget is mentioned at the end.
- **Patient names:** Mr Hollis and Pat are named as in your notes. Bridget may want to confirm they are happy to appear on the website, or have the names changed.
